summary: The Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program funds talented young Africans with financial need to study at partner universities in Africa, Canada, the US, the UK and elsewhere. It covers tuition, accommodation, books, mentoring, leadership development and a return flight. You do not apply to the Foundation: you apply to one partner university's own scholarship programme, and each partner has its own rules, dates and forms.
lookfor: Academic ability strong enough for the partner university's admission
Real financial need and barriers you have overcome (social, financial, personal, health)
A track record of leadership and community service
A clear commitment to give back to your community or country
Priority is often given to women, refugees and displaced people, and people with disabilities
cycle: No single deadline: each partner sets its own. Examples: Edinburgh 2027/28 — mandatory info sessions 15–24 Sep 2026, main application 19 Nov 2026, interviews Feb 2027, outcomes end of March 2027; McGill Fall 2027 is closed and reopens in spring 2027; Toronto's last graduate round closed 3 Nov 2025; UCT has historically closed 31 July. Check each partner page.

eligibility.q: Are you a citizen of an African country (and, for most partners, living in Africa)?
eligibility.no: This programme is only for Africans. Look at Chevening, Commonwealth or university scholarships instead.

eligibility.q: Can you show real financial need — that cost has limited your access to education?
eligibility.no: The programme targets economically disadvantaged applicants. Consider merit awards such as Türkiye Bursları or Stipendium Hungaricum.

eligibility.q: For master's: are you within the partner's age limit (Edinburgh, McGill and Toronto use 35 or under) and do you NOT already hold a master's degree?
eligibility.no: Most master's partners exclude people who already have a master's. Look at PhD funding or the Joint Japan/World Bank scholarship (for mid-career professionals).

eligibility.q: Do you have a record of leadership or community service you can describe?
eligibility.no: Start or deepen a community project now; it is central to selection. Apply in a later cycle.

eligibility.q: Can you meet the partner university's academic entry requirement (e.g. a UK 2:1 equivalent for Edinburgh)?
eligibility.no: Choose a partner whose entry level matches your grades, or an undergraduate partner if you have not finished a degree.

eligibility.q: Do you hold no citizenship or residency in the US, Canada, UK or EU (required by some partners, e.g. McGill)?
eligibility.no: Check the specific partner's rules; some exclude dual citizens or residents of those regions.

steps.title: Understand how the programme works
steps.why: Many applicants email the Foundation or wait for a single 'Mastercard deadline'. There is none — you apply through a partner institution.
do: Open the Foundation's Scholars Program page and read what is covered.
Open the 'Where to Apply' page and filter the partner list by level (undergraduate or master's).
Note that partners set their own deadlines and application fees (fees are reimbursed if you are selected).
Save the warning: the Foundation never asks individuals for payment.
tips: Write down two or three partners that offer your level and field.
avoid: Paying anyone who promises a Mastercard scholarship.
check: I can explain in one sentence how I will apply (through which partner).

steps.title: Shortlist partner universities and their windows
steps.why: Windows differ widely (some close in July, others in November). Picking partners whose dates you can meet is the first real decision.
do: For each partner on your list, open its own Mastercard Foundation page.
Record in a spreadsheet: level, eligible programmes, age limit, info-session dates, scholarship deadline, university admission deadline, interview period.
Master's examples: Edinburgh (UK), McGill and Toronto (Canada), Cambridge (UK), UCT and Pretoria (South Africa).
Undergraduate examples include Ashesi, KNUST, African Leadership University and UCT.
Pick 2–3 partners whose programmes fit your field and whose dates you can meet.
tips: Some partners only accept graduates of certain universities (Toronto's graduate round required a degree from an Africa Health Collaborative partner institution).
avoid: Choosing a programme the partner does not fund (e.g. Cambridge excludes MBA, MFin and some others).
check: I have 2–3 partners with dates and eligibility written down.

steps.title: Register for and attend the information session
steps.why: Several partners make the info session compulsory. At Edinburgh, if you register but do not attend, you are not invited to apply.
do: Check each partner page for info-session dates (Edinburgh: September; McGill: June–July; Toronto: October in the last round).
Register with the email you will use for the application.
Attend live, take notes on the essay questions, documents and timeline.
Save any confirmation email.
tips: If you missed this year's session, put next year's date in your calendar now and prepare your documents in the meantime.
check: I have attended (or booked) the session for each partner that requires it.

steps.title: Build your timeline for each partner
steps.why: Many partners have two linked processes — the scholarship form and the university admission — with different deadlines.
do: For each partner, list: info session, pre-screening/declaration form, scholarship deadline, university admission deadline, interviews, results.
Example (Edinburgh 2027/28): declaration form 19 Oct 2026, main application 19 Nov 2026, interviews from Feb 2027, outcome end of March 2027.
Example (McGill): stage 1 scholarship form in August, then university application by 1 December for pre-screened candidates.
Put each date in your calendar with reminders.
tips: Work back from the earliest deadline.
avoid: Assuming university admission and scholarship share one deadline.
check: Every date for every partner is in my calendar.

steps.title: Collect transcripts, degree certificate and ID
steps.why: Partners need official academic records; Edinburgh requires your degree certificate and transcript by the main deadline.
do: Request your official transcript from your university's Exams and Records office; ask for a scanned or emailed copy.
Scan your degree certificate (or statement of result). Undergraduate applicants: scan WAEC/NECO results.
Scan your passport data page. If you do not have one, start the application now (Nigeria: NIS e-passport portal).
Prepare proof of address if asked (UCT asks for it).
tips: Ask your registry how long transcripts take; some take weeks.
avoid: Waiting for the last week to request transcripts.
check: I have clear scans of transcript, certificate and passport.

steps.title: Prepare evidence of financial need and a CV
steps.why: Financial need is a core criterion. Some partners ask for a sworn statement; UCT asks for an affidavit witnessed by a commissioner of oaths.
do: Read the partner's form to see what evidence of need it asks for.
Gather simple proof: parents' or guardians' income, letters, or a sworn affidavit (in Nigeria, sworn at a High Court registry).
Write a 2-page CV focused on education, leadership, community service and work.
List each community activity with your role, dates and a result.
tips: Be honest and specific; vague hardship stories do not help.
check: I have need evidence ready and a 2-page CV.

steps.title: Check English requirements
steps.why: The scholarship may not need a test, but university admission might.
do: Read your programme's admission page for English rules.
Edinburgh: a test is not needed for the scholarship, but some applicants need one for admission depending on where they studied.
If you need a test, book IELTS/TOEFL early so results arrive before the admission deadline.
tips: Ask if an English-medium letter from your university is accepted.
avoid: Booking a test after the scholarship deadline.
check: I know whether I need a test and when I will take it.

steps.title: Write your personal story essay
steps.why: Partners want to understand the barriers you have faced and how you responded. This essay shows resilience and need.
do: Choose 1–2 real moments that shaped you (a barrier and how you dealt with it).
Structure: situation, what you did, what changed, what you learned.
Link the story to why education matters to you now.
Keep to the word limit in the form.
avoid: A sad story with no evidence of what you did.
check: A reader learns who I am and what I overcame.

steps.prompt: Your personal story (Edinburgh's form uses short essays on personal story, academic and leadership experience, and future ambition).
steps.limit: Set by each partner — check the current form

steps.title: Write your leadership and give-back essay
steps.why: Leadership, community service and a plan to give back are central to every partner's selection.
do: Pick your best leadership or service example: what problem, what you did, how many people it helped, what changed.
Explain what you will study and how it links to a problem at home.
Describe a concrete give-back plan after graduation (who, where, what).
If the partner focuses on a theme (Edinburgh: climate), show your experience or ambition there.
tips: Use numbers: people reached, money raised, hours given.
avoid: Big promises with no first step.
check: My essay names a real problem, my past action, and my future plan.
steps.prompt: Your academic and leadership experience and your future ambition / commitment to give back.
steps.limit: Set by each partner — check the current form

steps.title: Line up your referees
steps.why: Partners ask for academic or professional references; some collect them at different stages (Edinburgh asks only after interview shortlisting).
do: Choose two people who know you: lecturers, supervisors or mentors (not friends or family).
Send them your CV, essays and the partner's deadline.
Tell them how the partner collects references (portal email, upload, or later request).
Remind them a week before their deadline.
tips: Choose one referee who can speak about your community leadership.
avoid: Choosing a famous person who barely knows you.
check: Two referees have agreed and know the process.

steps.title: Submit the scholarship application
steps.why: Late or incomplete applications are not considered.
do: Log in to the partner's scholarship portal.
Complete each section: eligibility questions, personal details, education, activities, essays, uploads.
Proofread every answer and check names match your passport.
Submit and save the confirmation screen and email.
tips: Submit a few days early in case of internet or power problems.
avoid: Leaving the form as a draft.

steps.title: Submit the university admission application
steps.why: You must be admitted to the university. Some partners ask you to apply after pre-screening (McGill, Toronto), others in parallel (UCT).
do: Follow the partner's instruction on when to apply for admission.
Apply through the university's graduate or undergraduate portal and pay the fee if no waiver is given.
Upload transcripts, certificate, CV, statement and references as required.
Note your application number.
tips: Ask if you qualify for a fee waiver (McGill gives waivers to pre-screened candidates).
avoid: Applying to a programme the scholarship does not fund.
check: My admission application is submitted for an eligible programme.

steps.title: Prepare for the interview
steps.why: Shortlisted candidates are interviewed; at Edinburgh it is about 60 minutes by video (usually MS Teams).
do: Reread your essays and CV.
Prepare stories: a barrier you overcame, a leadership example, your give-back plan, why this programme.
Find a quiet room with stable internet and power backup.
Do a mock interview with someone who will give honest feedback.
tips: Speak about your community in specific terms: names of places, numbers, results.
check: I can tell my three key stories clearly in two minutes each.

steps.title: Accept, get your visa and prepare to travel
steps.why: The partner supports you through visas and arrival, but you must act quickly on every request.
do: Accept the scholarship and university offer by the stated dates.
Send any final documents the partner requests.
Apply for your student visa or study permit with the partner's support letter.
Attend pre-departure sessions.
tips: Keep copies of every document you send.
avoid: Booking flights before the partner confirms travel arrangements.
check: I have accepted and started my visa application.

faq.q: Can I apply directly to the Mastercard Foundation?
faq.a: No. You apply through a partner institution's own scholarship process.
No. Each partner sets its own; some close in July, others in November.

faq.q: Can I apply to several partners?
faq.a: Rules differ by partner. Read each partner's FAQ before applying to more than one.
No. The programme funds secondary, undergraduate and master's study.

faq.q: Do I need to pay an application fee?
faq.a: Partners may charge their usual fee, which is reimbursed if you are selected. The Foundation itself never asks for payment.
